title: Docker
intro: This part teaches containers from the ground up. You run other people's images, open one up to see its layers, and write a Dockerfile for hello-devops. Then you connect it to Redis with volumes, networks and Compose, and finish with a small, non-root, scanned image on GHCR. Everything after this, from CI pipelines to Kubernetes, ships the image you build here.

lessons.title: Containers: your first docker run
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain what a container is and how it differs from a VM, and run, inspect, stop and remove containers made from public images.

guess.q: You run `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx` on your Mac. Which kernel runs the nginx process?
options: Its own Debian kernel, booted inside the container
The macOS kernel, directly
The Linux kernel of a small VM that Docker Desktop runs
No kernel: Docker interprets the image like a JVM
guess.why: A container never boots a kernel of its own; it uses the host's Linux kernel. A Mac has no Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop runs one small Linux VM, and every container shares that VM's kernel.

sections.h: The problem: it works on my machine
sections.body:
Your code is only one part of what runs in production. The app also needs:

- a language runtime, such as Python 3.14
- libraries, such as Flask and gunicorn
- system packages from the operating system, such as OpenSSL
- settings, such as environment variables

Your laptop has one mix of these. The CI server has another, and the production server a third. A test passes on your Mac with Python 3.14 and fails in CI, where the runner has Python 3.12. Nothing in your code changed. The setup around it did.

Docker ships the setup together with the code. You build one package that holds the app and everything it needs. That exact package then runs on your Mac, on a CI runner and on a cloud server. On the Day 1 map, this is the package step.

The package is called an **image**: your app, its files and its settings, frozen and read-only. A running copy of an image is a **container**. Today you run images other people built. On Day 13 you build your own.

sections.h: A container is a process with blinkers and a budget
sections.body:
A virtual machine (VM) pretends to be a whole computer. It has virtual hardware and boots a full operating system with its own kernel. The kernel is the core of an operating system: it starts processes, hands out memory and talks to the hardware. Booting all of that takes many seconds, and each VM holds on to its own share of memory.

A container skips all of that. It is a normal Linux process, the same kind you listed with `ps` on Day 6. The kernel just gives it two extra things:

- Namespaces give the process a private view of the system: its own process list, network, hostname and files.
- cgroups (control groups) give it a budget: a cap on how much CPU and memory it may use.

So a container is a process with blinkers (namespaces) and a budget (cgroups). You can watch the blinkers work. `docker run --rm alpine ps` lists exactly one process, `ps` itself, running as PID 1. The machine runs hundreds of processes, and the container sees none of them.

No second kernel has to boot, so a container starts in about a second. The price is that every container on a host shares one kernel. A kernel bug can affect all of them. A container can also only run programs built for that kernel and that CPU.

sections.h: On a Mac, Docker runs a small Linux VM
sections.body:
macOS has its own kernel, and it is not Linux. So Docker Desktop starts one small Linux VM in the background, and every container you run lives inside it. Three pieces work together:

1. The `docker` command runs on your Mac. It is only a client that sends requests.
2. Docker Engine, a background program called `dockerd`, runs inside the VM. It pulls images and creates, starts and stops containers.
3. The VM's Linux kernel runs the container processes.

The client reaches the engine through a socket, the connection you set up on Day 2. Run `docker version` and it prints both halves: a Client section for the command on your Mac and a Server section that says `linux/arm64`.

That `arm64` is your CPU type, which Linux calls `aarch64`. Most cloud servers use amd64, also called `x86_64`. Popular images carry a variant for each CPU, and Docker picks the one that matches yours. An amd64-only image still runs on your Mac through emulation, only slower. On an amd64 server, an image with only arm64 code fails with `exec format error`. Day 12 shows how one image name can hold both variants.

Docker Desktop is free for personal use, education and small businesses. Companies with more than 250 employees or more than $10 million in yearly revenue need a paid subscription. Sign in with a free Docker account anyway: Docker Hub then lets you pull 200 images every 6 hours instead of 100.

sections.h: Images and containers: a class and its objects
sections.body:
An image and a container relate like a class and an object in Kotlin. The image is the class, a read-only definition. A container is an object made from it, with its own state. You can start ten containers from one image, and they do not affect each other.

Each container gets a thin writable layer on top of its image, and every file the app writes lands there. Remove the container and that layer goes with it. The image stays exactly as it was. Day 12 opens an image up and shows how the layers stack.

Images live in a registry, a server that stores images and hands them out. Docker Hub is the default one. When you run an image you do not have yet, Docker pulls (downloads) it first. An image name looks like `redis:8-alpine`: a name, a colon, and a tag that names a version. Leave the tag out and Docker uses `latest`, which is only a default label and does not promise the newest version.

sections.h: The docker run command, flag by flag
sections.body:
`docker run` creates a container from an image and starts it. Its shape is `docker run [options] image [command]`. Take `docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 -e TZ=UTC nginx`. Each option changes one thing:

- `-d` (detached) runs it in the background and prints the container ID.
- `--name web` names it, so later commands can say `web` instead of an ID.
- `-p 8080:80` publishes a port, explained in the next section.
- `-e TZ=UTC` sets an environment variable inside the container.
- `--rm` deletes the container when it stops, which suits one-off commands.
- `-it` connects your keyboard and a terminal, so you can type into a shell.

Anything after the image name replaces the image's default command. `docker run --rm alpine uname -m` runs `uname -m` instead of Alpine's shell. `docker run -it --rm ubuntu:24.04 bash` gives you the Ubuntu practice box from Part 1.

Once a container runs, three commands answer most questions:

- `docker ps` lists running containers.
- `docker logs web` shows what the main process printed, and `-f` keeps following it.
- `docker exec web <command>` runs an extra command inside the running container. `docker exec -it web sh` opens a shell there.

sections.h: Port mapping, explained
sections.body:
Each container has its own network namespace, and with it its own set of ports. Inside its container, nginx listens on port 80, where nothing on your Mac can reach it yet.

`-p 8080:80` connects the two. Read it as host first, then container: traffic to port 8080 on your Mac goes to port 80 in the container. Most people get this order backwards at first, so say it out loud a few times. `docker ps` shows the rule in its PORTS column as `0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp`.

A few rules follow from this:

- Two containers can both use port 80 inside, because each has its own namespace.
- A port on your Mac can belong to only one container at a time.
- The app inside must listen on `0.0.0.0`, as you saw on Day 8. An app bound to `127.0.0.1` only hears its own container.

That `0.0.0.0` in the PORTS column means Docker publishes the port on every network address of your Mac, so other devices on your Wi-Fi might reach it. On a laptop, `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` is the safer habit, because it keeps the port private to your Mac.

sections.h: The container lifecycle
sections.body:
A container moves through a few states:

1. Created: Docker has set it up but not started its process (`docker create`).
2. Running: its main process is alive.
3. Paused: the kernel has frozen its processes (`docker pause`). You will rarely need this.
4. Exited: the main process ended, by itself or because you stopped it.
5. Removed: `docker rm` deleted it and its writable layer.

A container lives exactly as long as its main process, PID 1. When that process ends, the container exits, and its exit code tells you how. 0 means success. `docker ps -a` shows any other number, as in `Exited (3)`, and `docker logs` still shows what the process printed before it died.

`docker stop` sends SIGTERM to PID 1, waits 10 seconds, then sends SIGKILL. You met these signals on Day 6, and Kubernetes stops containers the same way. A process killed by SIGKILL exits with 137, which is 128 plus 9, the number of SIGKILL. In the worked example, `sleep` runs as PID 1, ignores SIGTERM and ends with exactly that code after 10 seconds. Day 13 explains why.

Stopping deletes nothing. An exited container keeps its files, and `docker start` runs it again. Only `docker rm` throws it away.

lessons.analogy: A container is like an apartment in a big building. Each apartment has its own front door, address and mailbox, so the people inside cannot see their neighbours: those are the namespaces. Each one also has its own meters for water and power, with a limit: those are the cgroups. All apartments stand on one foundation and share the building's pipes, which is the kernel. The picture fails on speed. Nobody builds an apartment in one second, and Docker builds a container that fast because nothing new has to be built, only fenced off.

code.title: check-docker.sh (keep it in ~/code, outside the repo)
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Checks that Docker works and shows which CPU type your containers use.
set -euo pipefail

echo "Docker client and server:"
docker version --format 'client {{.Client.Version}}, server {{.Server.Version}} ({{.Server.Os}}/{{.Server.Arch}})'

echo "CPU type inside a container:"
docker run --rm alpine uname -m

echo "Processes a container can see:"
docker run --rm alpine ps

echo "Containers on this machine (running and stopped):"
docker ps -a --format '{{.Names}}  {{.Image}}  {{.Status}}'

The rule is `-p HOST:CONTAINER`: the left number is on your Mac, and the right number is where the app listens in the container. explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate what happens when you type `docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx` on a Mac, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention the image, the registry, the Linux VM, namespaces and the port mapping.
explain_back.answer: Docker looks for the nginx image on my machine and, if it is missing, pulls it from Docker Hub, the default registry. Docker Engine then starts a container inside the small Linux VM that Docker Desktop runs, because containers need a Linux kernel. The container is just an nginx process that namespaces fence off and cgroups can limit. The `-d` flag runs it in the background, and `-p 8080:80` sends traffic from port 8080 on my Mac to port 80 inside the container, where nginx listens.

check.q: You want two web containers that both listen on port 80 inside. Which way of publishing them works?
options: `-p 80:80` for both containers
`-p 8080:80` for one, `-p 8081:80` for the other
`-p 80:8080` for one, `-p 80:8081` for the other
No `-p` at all; curl port 80 on localhost

check.q: A teammate edits a config file inside a running container with `docker exec`, then runs `docker rm` and a fresh `docker run` from the same image. Where is the edit?
options: In the image, because exec writes to the image
On Docker Hub, because Docker syncs changes
Still there, because containers share files
Gone, because it lived in the removed container
check.why: Changes go to the container's writable layer, which `docker rm` deletes; the image never changes.

check.q: A batch job container shows `Exited (137)` after someone ran `docker stop` on it. What does that tell you?
options: The job ignored SIGTERM and was killed with SIGKILL
The job finished its work and exited normally
Docker ran out of disk space while stopping it
The image was built for a different CPU type
check.why: 137 is 128 plus 9, and signal 9 is SIGKILL, which Docker sends when SIGTERM did not end the process within 10 seconds.

interview.q: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
interview.a: A virtual machine runs a full operating system with its own kernel on virtual hardware, so it is heavy and slow to boot. A container is a normal process on a Linux host that the kernel isolates with namespaces and limits with cgroups. Containers share the host kernel, so they start in about a second and use little memory. The trade-off is weaker isolation: a kernel bug can affect every container on the host, which is why some platforms wrap containers in small VMs.

interview.q: What happens when you run `docker stop`, and why does it matter?
interview.a: Docker sends SIGTERM to the container's main process and waits, 10 seconds by default. A well-written app catches SIGTERM, finishes the requests it is handling and exits cleanly. If the process is still running after the wait, Docker sends SIGKILL, which ends it at once and can lose work; the exit code is then 137. Kubernetes stops pods the same way, so the same SIGTERM handling protects you in both places.

interview.q: Why does an image built on an Apple Silicon Mac sometimes fail on a cloud server?
interview.a: Containers run on the host's kernel and CPU, so the code inside must match the server's CPU type. A Mac builds arm64 code by default, while most cloud servers are amd64. If the image only holds arm64 code, the server fails with `exec format error`. The fix is a multi-platform image that holds a variant for each CPU, which `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` creates.

deeper.body:
Three small experiments let you watch namespaces, cgroups and CPU types at work.

Start with the process namespace. Run `docker run --rm alpine ps`. The output lists exactly one process: `ps` itself, as PID 1. Your Mac and the Linux VM run hundreds of processes, but the container cannot see any of them. Now run `docker run --rm alpine hostname`. You get a random-looking name such as `89851d1cc476`, the container's short ID. The container has its own hostname namespace too. Then `docker run --rm alpine ip addr` shows a third namespace: the container has its own loopback and its own `eth0` with a private address such as `172.17.0.3`.

For cgroups, start Redis with a memory limit: `docker run -d --name capped -m 64m redis:8-alpine`. Then run `docker stats --no-stream capped`. When we ran it, the MEM USAGE / LIMIT column said `8.633MiB / 64MiB`. If Redis tried to use more than 64 MB, the kernel would stop it. Remove it with `docker rm -f capped`. The Kubernetes memory limits on Day 35 use this same kernel feature.

For CPU types, run `docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 alpine uname -m` on your Mac. It prints `x86_64`. The container really runs amd64 code, translated as it runs by an emulator inside Docker Desktop. That is fine for a quick test and too slow for heavy work. Without an emulator, the same trick fails. On an amd64 Linux server with no emulator installed, `docker run --platform linux/arm64 alpine uname -m` printed `exec /bin/uname: exec format error`. That is the exact error a server shows when someone ships an arm64-only image to it.

Docker Desktop has two settings worth knowing here. Under Settings, General, you can choose the virtual machine manager. Another setting uses Apple's Rosetta to speed up amd64 emulation. Docker Desktop is also not your only choice. OrbStack and Colima run a Linux VM too and give you the same `docker` command, so this course works with them as well. For a friendly tour of the kernel features behind all this, read [Julia Evans' post on containers](https://jvns.ca/blog/2016/10/10/what-even-is-a-container/).

options: The same size, because the file is gone
Smaller, because rm also cleans the cache
It depends on whether you run docker image prune
About 50 MB bigger, even though the file is deleted

terms.plain: A read-only set of file changes (added, changed or deleted files) that stacks on the layers below it.
A JSON file in an image with its settings: default command, environment variables, user and the list of layers.
A JSON file that lists an image's config and layers by their digests.
A sha256 hash of some content, such as a layer or a manifest; the same content always has the same digest.
The rule that a file from the image is copied up into the container's own layer the first time it changes.
A list of manifests, one per CPU type, behind one image name; also called a manifest list.
A server that stores images and hands them out, such as Docker Hub or ghcr.io.
A movable, human-friendly label for an image, such as 1.0.0 or latest.

sections.h: What is inside an image
sections.body:
When you pull an image it looks like one thing. Inside, it is a small bundle of parts:

- Layers: each layer is an archive of file changes compared with the layer below. Files can be added, changed or deleted.
- A config: a JSON file with the image's settings, such as the default command, environment variables, working folder and user. It also lists the layers in order.
- A manifest: a JSON file that points to the config and to every layer by their digest, which the next section explains.

Dockerfile instructions that change files, such as `RUN` and `COPY`, each create a layer. Instructions that only change settings, such as `CMD`, `ENV` and `EXPOSE`, only edit the config. That is why `docker history` lists them with a size of 0B.

Try it on the base image you will use on Day 13. The command `docker image inspect python:3.14-slim --format '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}'` printed four layer digests on the day we checked. Then `docker history python:3.14-slim` shows which instruction made each one: 87.7 MB of Debian files at the bottom, 42.1 MB for the Python build, and two small layers.

If you know git, the picture is familiar. Layers are like immutable snapshots of changes, and the manifest is like a commit that points at them.

sections.h: Layers are named by their content
sections.body:
A digest is a sha256 hash of some bytes, written as `sha256:` followed by 64 hexadecimal characters. Docker names every layer, config and manifest by its digest. This is called content addressing: the name comes from the content itself. Three things follow:

- The same content gets the same name on every machine.
- Change one byte, and the name changes.
- Docker can check a download by hashing it again and comparing.

The big win is sharing. Two images built `FROM python:3.14-slim` start with the same four layers, so your disk and the registry store them once. We built two such images, each adding one small file. `docker system df -v` listed each at 178 MB, but only 16.84 kB of each was unique. The other 178.3 MB were shared.

Pushes and pulls skip shared layers too. In the worked example you will see `Already exists` and `Layer already exists` instead of a download.

This is also why the order of a Dockerfile matters, as Day 13 shows. Docker reuses a layer only when everything below it is identical.

refs.title: Storage drivers: images, layers and the container layer

sections.h: The container layer and copy-on-write
sections.body:
Image layers are read-only. When Docker starts a container, it adds one thin writable layer on top. A union filesystem then shows all the layers as one folder tree. On Linux that is OverlayFS: it stacks the image layers under the container layer and shows you the merged view.

Reads and writes follow four rules:

1. A read looks from the top layer down and uses the first copy of the file it finds.
2. The first write to a file from the image copies the whole file up into the container layer. Later writes change that copy. This is **copy-on-write**.
3. A new file goes straight into the container layer.
4. A delete adds a small marker called a whiteout, which hides the file below. The bytes below stay where they are.

`docker diff` lists what a container changed, with A for added, C for changed and D for deleted. We edited `nginx.conf`, created a file in `/tmp` and deleted `50x.html` in an nginx container. The diff showed exactly those, plus files nginx wrote at startup, such as `/run/nginx.pid`. Then `docker ps --size` reported that container layer as `106kB (virtual 177MB)`: 106 kB of its own on top of 177 MB of shared image.

Copy-on-write has a cost. Copying a big file up is slow, and the layer dies with the container. That is why databases keep their files in volumes (Day 14).

sections.h: Deleting a file never shrinks an image
sections.body:
Here is the trap that follows from layers. One `RUN` step creates a 50 MB file, and the next `RUN` step deletes it. The second layer only adds a whiteout. The 50 MB still sit in the first layer and ship with every pull.

We built both versions on `alpine:3.22`. The image that created and deleted the file in two steps had a content size of 53.8 MB. The one that did both in a single `RUN` had 3.8 MB. There are two fixes:

- Create and clean up in the same `RUN`, joined with `&&`.
- Use a multi-stage build (Day 16) and copy only the results into a fresh stage.

[dive](https://github.com/wagoodman/dive) makes waste visible. It walks an image layer by layer, shows what each layer adds, and estimates wasted space. Install it with `brew install dive`. With `CI=true` it prints a pass or fail report, and for the two-step image it said: efficiency 14%, 50 MB wasted in `/big.bin`, FAIL.

`docker image ls` shows two sizes on current Docker. CONTENT SIZE is the compressed data, close to what you download and push. DISK USAGE also counts the unpacked copy on disk, so it is bigger.

Size is worth watching for three reasons:

- Every deploy and every CI run pulls the image.
- It takes disk space on every machine that runs it.
- Every extra package is one more thing to patch.

sections.h: Registries, repositories, tags and digests
sections.body:
A registry stores images and hands them out. You will meet:

- Docker Hub (`docker.io`), the default
- GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`), next to your code on GitHub
- cloud registries: Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry and Google Artifact Registry
- a registry you run yourself, such as the `registry:3` image in the worked example

A full image name can have five parts, as in `ghcr.io/ana/hello-devops:1.0.0@sha256:...`: the registry, a namespace (user or organisation), the repository, a tag and a digest. Leave parts out and Docker fills in defaults, so `nginx` means `docker.io/library/nginx:latest`. The `library` namespace holds Docker Official Images.

A tag is a movable label. Anyone who can push can point `1.0` at a different image tomorrow, and the worked example does exactly that. A digest is the hash of the manifest, so it always means one exact image. `docker pull nginx@sha256:...` gives you the same bytes every time. Teams pin digests in deploy files so the image they tested is the image that runs. Think of a tag as a git branch name and a digest as a commit SHA.

Publishing takes three commands: `docker login` to the registry, `docker tag` to give the image its full name, and `docker push`. The push prints the digest on its last line. Day 16 pushes hello-devops to ghcr.io.

Docker Hub limits pulls per 6 hours: 100 without signing in, counted per IP address, and 200 when you are signed in.

sections.h: One name, many CPUs: the image index
sections.body:
A multi-platform image adds one more JSON file on top: an image index, also called a manifest list. It lists one manifest per platform, meaning an operating system plus a CPU type. When you pull, the registry sends the index first, and Docker picks the manifest for your machine. On your Mac that is `linux/arm64`.

`docker buildx imagetools inspect python:3.14-slim` reads the index straight from the registry without pulling anything. On the day we checked, it listed eight platforms, among them `linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64/v8`, `linux/arm/v7` and `linux/s390x`. Next to each platform sat an entry marked `unknown/unknown`. Those are attestations: records of how the image was built, which Docker's builder adds by default. Day 52 uses them.

If your CPU is missing from the index, the image runs only through emulation, or not at all, and fails with `exec format error`. The worked example builds a small two-platform image and shows its index.

Docker Engine 29 also changed where images live. Fresh installs and Docker Desktop use the containerd image store, which can keep several platforms of one image on your machine. `docker image ls --tree` shows them as a tree under each name.

refs.title: containerd image store with Docker Engine

sections.h: Official images and Docker Hardened Images
sections.body:
Every image you build starts from someone else's image, so pick bases you can trust. On Docker Hub, look for these labels:

- Docker Official Images, such as `python`, `nginx` and `redis`, in the `library` namespace.
- Verified Publisher images, which software vendors publish themselves.

Docker Hardened Images (DHI) are a newer option. Docker sold them from May 2025 and made the catalog free and open source, under the Apache 2.0 licence, in December 2025. From Docker's docs:

- They come from `dhi.io`. You run `docker login dhi.io` with a free Docker account, then pull images such as `dhi.io/python:3.13`.
- Runtime images are distroless: no shell and no package manager, and they run as a non-root user by default.
- `-dev` variants add a shell and package manager for build stages.
- Every image comes with signed records of what is inside it and how it was built.

Docker says this approach cuts the attack surface by up to 95%. That figure is Docker's own claim, not an independent measurement. Day 16 shows how a hardened base would change the hello-devops Dockerfile.

lessons.analogy: Think of an overhead projector with a stack of transparent sheets. Each sheet adds some drawings, and the screen shows all of them at once: those are the layers. A container adds one blank sheet on top for its own notes. To erase a line drawn on a lower sheet, you can only stick a white patch over it on a higher sheet. The line is hidden but still there, and the stack is no lighter. The picture breaks on sharing: a real sheet sits in one stack at a time, while Docker uses the same layer in many images at once.

steps: Create `~/code/docker-play/bloat/Dockerfile` from the Files section. Build it as `bloat:1.0` and read `docker history bloat:1.0`. Which row holds the 50 MB?

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences what happens when you pull `nginx` on your Mac and then start two containers from it. Mention the index, layers, digests and the writable layer.
explain_back.answer: Docker reads `nginx` as `docker.io/library/nginx:latest` and asks Docker Hub for that tag, which points to an image index. From the index it picks the manifest for linux/arm64, then downloads the config and every layer it does not already have, checking each by its digest. Both containers share those read-only layers on disk, and each gets its own thin writable layer on top. Anything a container writes goes into its own layer through copy-on-write, so the two never see each other's changes and the image never changes.

recap: An image is read-only layers plus a config, tied together by a manifest.
Everything is named by a sha256 digest of its content, so identical layers are stored and sent once.
A container adds one writable layer; the first write to an image file copies it up.
Deleting a file in a later layer hides it but never shrinks the image.
Tags move and digests do not; pin a digest when you need the exact same image.
An image index holds one manifest per CPU type, and Docker picks yours when it pulls.

Two copies, one per repository
Nothing; registries store only your own layers
A compressed diff between the two images

check.q: A deploy file says `image: shop:2.3`. Last night someone pushed a broken build with the same tag. What would have protected the deploy?
options: Using the tag latest instead
Running docker image prune before deploying

options: Docker compresses the file on each write
The file is copied up into the container layer and lost with the container
Writes go back into the image, which grows each day
Docker refuses to write to files that came from the image
check.why: The first write copies the whole file into the container's writable layer, which is slow for big files and is deleted along with the container.

interview.q: What is an image layer, and why do layers matter?
interview.a: A layer is a read-only set of file changes, usually made by one Dockerfile instruction, and named by the sha256 digest of its content. An image is a stack of layers plus a config, listed in a manifest. Because layers are content-addressed, identical layers are stored once and skipped on push and pull, which saves disk and time. They also explain two common surprises: deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image, and a change in one layer forces every later layer to rebuild.

interview.q: What is the difference between a tag and a digest?
interview.a: A tag is a human-friendly name such as `1.0.0` or `latest`, and anyone with push rights can move it to a different image. A digest is the sha256 hash of the image's manifest, so it always means exactly the same content. Deploying by digest makes deploys repeatable and protects you from a tag that changed underneath you. Teams often keep both: a readable tag for people and a digest in deploy files.

interview.q: How can one image name work on both an Apple Silicon laptop and an Intel server?
interview.a: The name points to an image index, also called a manifest list, rather than a single manifest. The index has one manifest per platform, such as linux/amd64 and linux/arm64, each with its own config and layers. When a machine pulls, Docker reads the index and downloads only the variant for its own CPU. You build such an image with `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push`.

deeper.body:
A registry is just a web server with a small HTTP API, so you can read an image by hand with curl. Day 9's HTTP skills apply directly. Start the registry from the worked example again and push the two-platform `hello:multi` image to it.

First ask for the index. The `Accept` header tells the registry which JSON format you want:

`curl -s -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json' localhost:5001/v2/hello/manifests/multi | jq '.manifests[].platform.architecture'`

When we did this, the answer listed `amd64`, `arm64` and two `unknown` entries, which are the attestations. Each entry also has a `digest`. Copy the arm64 digest and ask for that manifest, this time with the header `Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json`, at `localhost:5001/v2/hello/manifests/<digest>`. The manifest names one config digest and two layer digests: the Alpine base and the layer that holds `hello.txt`.

Finally fetch the config itself from `localhost:5001/v2/hello/blobs/<config digest>` and pipe it into `jq '{architecture, os}'`. Ours said `"architecture": "arm64"` and `"os": "linux"`, with the command `cat /hello.txt`. Every object came from a URL that ends in its own digest. That is content addressing in practice: the client can hash what it got and check it against the name it asked for.

Two more details are worth knowing on current Docker.

- With the containerd image store, an image's ID is the digest of its index. That is why `docker build` output ends with `exporting manifest list sha256:...` and `docker history` shows the same first 12 characters.
- `docker image ls` on Engine 29 hides untagged images and collapses platforms; add `--all` or `--tree` to see everything.

The [OverlayFS driver page](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/overlayfs-driver/) shows how the layers become one folder tree on disk.

guess.q: A Dockerfile does `COPY . .` and then `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`. You change one comment in app.py and rebuild. What happens?
options: Only app.py is copied again; pip install is reused
pip install runs again, because a layer above it changed
Docker rebuilds everything, including the base image
Nothing changes until you delete the old image
guess.why: A changed layer invalidates every layer after it, and `COPY . .` changes whenever any file changes. Copy requirements.txt and install first, then copy the code, so code edits skip the slow install.

terms.plain: A text file of instructions that tells Docker how to build an image, read from top to bottom.
The image a Dockerfile starts from with FROM, such as python:3.14-slim.
The folder you pass to docker build; COPY can only take files from inside it.
Layers saved from earlier builds, reused when an instruction and everything before it are unchanged.

sections.h: A Dockerfile is a recipe Docker follows from top to bottom
sections.body:
Docker builds an image by following a plain text file named `Dockerfile`. It runs the instructions in order, and each one starts from the result of the one before. Each instruction that changes files adds a layer, exactly the layers you inspected on Day 12.

The Dockerfile lives in git next to the app, and teammates review changes to it like any other code. That is the Day 1 idea of everything as code, applied to packaging.

You build with `docker build -t hello-devops:1.0.0 .`. The `-t` flag names and tags the result, and the final dot is the build context, which has its own section below. The builder behind `docker build` is called BuildKit. It is the default in Docker Desktop and Docker Engine, and it is the program that prints the `[+] Building` progress you will see in the worked example.

Today you write a Dockerfile with one stage that runs as root. It is the right first step, because every line is easy to see. Day 16 turns it into the multi-stage, non-root version that the lab ships.

sections.h: The instructions you will use
sections.body:
Most Dockerfiles use a handful of instructions:

- `FROM` picks the base image to start from, such as `python:3.14-slim`.
- `WORKDIR` sets the folder that later instructions work in, and creates it.
- `COPY` copies files from the build context into the image. `ADD` can also fetch URLs and unpack archives; prefer `COPY` unless you need that.
- `RUN` runs a command at build time, such as `pip install`, and saves the result as a layer.
- `ENV` sets an environment variable for later steps and for the running container.
- `ARG` declares a variable that exists only during the build.
- `EXPOSE` documents the port the app listens on. It publishes nothing; `-p` does that.
- `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` set what the container runs when it starts.

Two more arrive on Day 16. The `USER` instruction picks the user the app runs as, and `HEALTHCHECK` tells Docker how to test the app. The `LABEL` instruction adds key and value notes to the image, such as a link to its source repo.

Read the Day 13 Dockerfile in the Files section with this list next to it. Every line is one of these instructions, with a comment that says why it is there.

sections.h: The build context and .dockerignore
sections.body:
The dot in `docker build -t hello-devops:1.0.0 .` is the **build context**: the folder whose files the build may use. A `COPY` can only take files from inside it, so `COPY ../secrets.txt .` fails. Docker also looks for the file named `Dockerfile` in that folder, unless you name another one with `-f`.

A `.dockerignore` file in that folder lists files the build must never see, with patterns like `.gitignore`. The lab's file keeps out:

- `.git` and `.github`, the repo's history and workflows
- `.venv` and Python caches, which belong to your Mac only
- folders for later days, such as `infra`, `k8s` and `chart`
- Markdown files, which the app does not need

Our Dockerfile copies two files by name, so for now the ignore file is a safety net. It starts to matter the day someone writes `COPY . .`. In a test, a folder with a 10 MB `.venv` sent `10.00MB` of context to the builder on every build. After adding `.venv` to `.dockerignore`, the same build sent 100 bytes. Without the ignore file, `COPY . .` would also bake your `.git` folder and any local secret files into the image.

sections.h: The build cache, and why order matters
sections.body:
Docker keeps every layer it builds in its build cache. On the next build it checks each instruction in order. If the instruction and everything before it are unchanged, Docker reuses the saved layer and prints `CACHED`. If something changed, Docker rebuilds that layer and every layer after it, even ones whose instructions did not change. That second half trips most people up. Think of a row of dominoes: tip one over and everything after it falls.

What counts as changed depends on the instruction:

- For `COPY` and `ADD`, Docker checks the contents of the files. Their modification time is ignored, so `touch app.py` changes nothing.
- For `RUN`, Docker only compares the command text. `RUN apt-get update` stays cached for months, even if new packages exist.

So order the steps from rarely changed to often changed:

1. `FROM` the base image.
2. `COPY requirements.txt` on its own.
3. `RUN pip install`, the slow step.
4. `COPY app.py`, which changes all the time.

With this order, a code edit rebuilds only the last small layer. In the worked example that rebuild takes 0.3 seconds, against about 10 seconds for a fresh pip install.

sections.h: CMD, ENTRYPOINT and who is PID 1
sections.body:
`CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` both say what runs when a container starts. They differ in how `docker run` arguments treat them:

- `CMD` is a default. Anything you type after the image name replaces it.
- `ENTRYPOINT` is fixed. Anything you type after the image name is added to it as arguments.
- With both, `ENTRYPOINT` is the program and `CMD` gives its default arguments.

A tiny image with `ENTRYPOINT ["echo", "Hello,"]` and `CMD ["world"]` shows it. `docker run greeter` printed `Hello, world`, and `docker run greeter Ana` printed `Hello, Ana`. `--entrypoint` swaps the program itself. For a web app, `CMD` alone is the simple choice.

Write both in exec form, a JSON list such as `["gunicorn", "app:app"]`. Then your app runs directly as PID 1 and receives the SIGTERM from `docker stop`. In shell form, `CMD gunicorn app:app`, Docker runs `/bin/sh -c "gunicorn app:app"`. The shell becomes PID 1 and does not pass SIGTERM on. We measured both. The shell-form container needed 10.2 seconds to stop and ended with code 137. The exec-form one stopped in 0.6 seconds with code 0. PID 1 is also special in Linux: it gets no default signal handlers, which is why `sleep` ignored SIGTERM on Day 11.

sections.h: ARG, ENV and config from the environment
sections.body:
`ARG` and `ENV` both set variables, at different times:

- `ARG` exists only while the image builds. You set it with `--build-arg NAME=value`.
- `ENV` is stored in the image and is present when the container runs. `docker run -e NAME=value` overrides it.

A test image showed the difference. With `--build-arg BUILD_NOTE=hello`, a `RUN` step printed `at build time: hello`, and the running container printed `at run time: not set`. To keep a build value, copy it: `ARG APP_VERSION` followed by `ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION`, as our Dockerfile does.

One warning before you reach for either one: `docker history` shows ARG values in plain text, so never pass passwords or tokens this way. Day 16 shows the safe way.

Why put settings in the environment at all? [The Twelve-Factor App](https://12factor.net/config) is a well-known set of rules for web apps. Its config rule says to keep settings that change between deploys out of the code, in environment variables. Then one image runs in every environment, and only the variables differ. hello-devops reads four of them:

- `APP_VERSION`, the version it reports
- `GREETING`, the message it returns
- `REDIS_HOST`, where Redis runs (empty means count in memory)
- `PORT`, used only when you run `python app.py`

`PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` is not one of the app's settings. It makes Python print log lines at once, so `docker logs` shows them as they happen.

sections.h: Tags, build checks and docker init
sections.body:
Tag your own images with real versions, such as `1.0.0`; Day 17 explains version numbers. Leave the tag out and Docker uses `latest`, which only means whatever was built last. In `FROM`, name a specific base such as `python:3.14-slim`, never bare `python`, or your build gets whatever `latest` points to on the day you build. One image can carry several tags: `docker tag hello-devops:1.0.0 hello-devops:stable` adds a second name and copies nothing.

`docker build --check .` lints a Dockerfile without building it. We ran it on a file with three common slips, and it named each with a line number:

- `FromAsCasing`: `FROM ... as base` mixes upper and lower case
- `LegacyKeyValueFormat`: `ENV GREETING Hello` should be `ENV GREETING=Hello`
- `JSONArgsRecommended`: a shell-form `CMD`, with the signal problem from above

`docker init`, which ships with Docker Desktop, writes a starter `Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore`, `compose.yaml` and `README.Docker.md` for a project. It has templates for Python, Go, Java, Node and more. It is a fine way to get a second opinion, but read every line before you keep it. Run it in an empty folder, because it overwrites files and you cannot get them back.

lessons.analogy: Picture a layered cake, with the build cache as a fridge full of finished layers. Change only the decoration on top, and every lower layer comes out of the fridge ready. Change the sponge at the bottom, and every layer above it has to be baked again. A real baker could keep an upper layer after changing a lower one. Docker never does: everything after the first change gets rebuilt.

code.title: Dockerfile (Day 13 version: one stage; the lab keeps it as docker/Dockerfile.simple)
code.src:
# Day 13 version: one stage, runs as root. Day 16 replaces it.
FROM python:3.14-slim

# Work in /app inside the image. Docker creates the folder.
WORKDIR /app

# Copy the dependency list first, so the slow install step is cached.
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Now copy the code. Editing app.py only rebuilds from here down.
COPY app.py .

# The version is set at build time: docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.0.0 .
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

# Document the port the app listens on. This does not publish it.
EXPOSE 8000

# Exec form (a JSON list): gunicorn runs as PID 1 and receives SIGTERM.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "2", "app:app"]
code.run: docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.0.0 -t hello-devops:1.0.0 . && docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 hello-devops:1.0.0

Running the same build twice in a row
Changing a file listed in .dockerignore
Adding a dependency to build.gradle.kts

`curl --help -s https://example.com`
`-s https://example.com` on its own
`curl --help` only

check.q: A teammate's container takes exactly 10 seconds to stop every time and exits with 137. Its Dockerfile ends with `CMD python server.py`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add EXPOSE for the server's port
Run the container with more memory
Write CMD as ["python", "server.py"]
Move the CMD line to the top of the file
check.why: In shell form a shell is PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM, so Docker waits 10 seconds and sends SIGKILL; exec form makes Python PID 1.

interview.q: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
interview.a: Both define what runs when a container starts. ENTRYPOINT sets the program, and arguments given to `docker run` are added after it. CMD sets the default command or default arguments, and anything you type after the image name replaces it. A common pattern is ENTRYPOINT for the binary and CMD for its default flags. Either way, use the exec form, a JSON list, so the app runs as PID 1 and receives signals like SIGTERM.

interview.q: How do you make Docker builds fast?
interview.a: Order instructions from least to most often changed, so the cache gets reused: base image, dependency files, install, then source code. Copy only the files you need and keep a .dockerignore, so unrelated changes stop breaking the cache and the context stays small. A small base image means less to download and push. In CI, share the build cache between runs, because every fresh runner starts with an empty one.

interview.q: What is the difference between ARG and ENV?
interview.a: ARG is a build-time variable that you set with `--build-arg`; it is gone when the container runs. ENV is stored in the image and is present in every container, where `docker run -e` can override it. To keep a build value at run time, copy it from ARG into ENV. Neither is safe for secrets, because both show up in the image history or config; build secrets go through secret mounts instead.

deeper.body:
Run the PID 1 experiment yourself. Make a folder with a two-line Dockerfile: `FROM hello-devops:1.0.0` and then `CMD gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 2 app:app`, in shell form. Build it as `shell:1.0` and start one container from it and one from your real image. Then look at PID 1 in each with `docker exec <name> cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '`:

- In the shell-form container, PID 1 was `/bin/sh -c gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 2 app:app`.
- In the real image, PID 1 was `/usr/local/bin/python3.14 /usr/local/bin/gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 2 app:app`.

Now time `docker stop` on each with `time docker stop <name>`. When we tried it, the shell-form container took 10.2 seconds and ended as `Exited (137)`. The exec-form container stopped in 0.6 seconds and ended as `Exited (0)`. The shell got the SIGTERM and did nothing with it, so after 10 seconds Docker sent SIGKILL. In production, every deploy then waits 10 extra seconds per container, and requests in flight are cut off.

Sometimes you need a shell script as the entry point, for example to wait for a database or to build a config file first. End such a script with `exec "$@"` or `exec gunicorn ...`. The `exec` replaces the shell with your app, so the app becomes PID 1. Another option is `docker run --init`, which adds a tiny init program as PID 1 that forwards signals.

One more cache detail surprised us while testing. We added a comment to app.py, rebuilt, removed it, and later added the very same comment again. The second time, the `COPY app.py` step said CACHED. The cache is keyed by file contents, so a version of the file that was built before matches its old layer, even after other builds in between. That is also why `touch` alone never triggers a rebuild.

The [Dockerfile reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/) has a table that shows every combination of CMD and ENTRYPOINT in exec and shell form.

lessons.title: Volumes and networks
lessons.goal: By the end you can keep data safe in volumes, choose between volumes, bind mounts and tmpfs, and connect containers on a user-defined network where they find each other by name.

guess.q: Two containers, `api` and `db`, run on Docker's default network. Inside api, `ping db` runs. What happens?
options: It fails with a bad address: the default network has no lookup by name
It works, because Docker registers every container name
It works, but only if db was started with -p
It works on a Mac and fails on Linux
guess.why: Only user-defined networks have Docker's built-in DNS server. On the default bridge, containers can reach each other by IP address only.

sections.h: Containers are disposable, so where does data live?
sections.body:
On Day 12 you saw where a container's own files go: into its thin writable layer, which `docker rm` deletes. That is what you want. You should be able to throw away any container and start a fresh one, for an upgrade or after a crash.

So data you care about must live outside the container. Docker gives you three kinds of mounts, which attach storage at a folder inside the container. Pick by asking who owns the data:

- Docker owns it, such as a database's files: use a volume.
- You own it, such as source code you edit on your Mac: use a bind mount.
- Nobody should keep it, such as a temporary token: use a tmpfs mount.

Volumes also fix a speed problem. Writes into the container layer go through copy-on-write, which is slow for big, busy files. A volume skips the layers and writes straight to the disk.

hello-devops has a data problem right now. The visit count lives in memory, so every restart resets it to zero. Gunicorn also runs two worker processes, and each keeps its own count, so the number can jump back. Moving the count into Redis fixes both: the workers share one number, and Redis keeps it in a volume.

sections.h: Volumes: storage Docker manages
sections.body:
A named volume is created with `docker volume create notes`, or on the fly by `docker run -v notes:/data ...`. The left side of `-v` is the volume name and the right side is the folder inside the container. The same volume can be mounted into a new container later, and the data is still there.

A few behaviours are worth knowing before they surprise you:

- A new, empty volume mounted over a folder that has files in the image gets a copy of those files. Mount an empty volume at nginx's html folder, and `index.html` and `50x.html` appear in it.
- `-v /data` with no name creates an anonymous volume with a random 64-character ID. Some images, such as `registry:3`, declare one in their Dockerfile, so you get one without asking.
- Anonymous volumes stay behind after `docker rm`. Use `--rm`, or `docker rm -v`, to delete them with the container.
- `docker volume inspect` shows a mount point under `/var/lib/docker/volumes`. On a Mac that path is inside Docker Desktop's VM, and Docker's docs say not to touch it directly.

`--mount type=volume,source=notes,target=/data` is the long form of the same thing. It is wordier and harder to get wrong, so many teams use it in scripts.

To back up a volume, mount it into a throwaway container next to a folder from your Mac and run `tar` there. The lab's `docker/volume-backup.sh` does exactly that, and it restores the archive into another volume too.

sections.h: Bind mounts, tmpfs and file ownership
sections.body:
A bind mount shows a folder from your Mac inside the container: `-v "$PWD/site":/usr/share/nginx/html`. A path on the left side means a bind mount, and a plain name means a volume. Both sides see every change at once, which is great while you edit code. Add `:ro` to make the mount read-only inside the container.

Two things bite people:

- A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path. Mount an empty folder over nginx's html folder, and nginx serves nothing.
- On a Mac, files cross from macOS into Docker's Linux VM through a file sharing layer called VirtioFS. Folders with many small files can be slower than a volume.

File ownership works by user ID numbers, not names. On a Linux machine, such as a CI runner, a container running as user 10001 tried to write into a bind-mounted folder owned by root. It failed with `touch: /out/from-10001.txt: Permission denied`. A file written by a root container showed up on the host owned by uid 0. Docker Desktop on a Mac hides most of this, because its file sharing makes files look like yours. So a setup that works on your laptop can still fail in CI. Day 6's permission rules explain every case.

A tmpfs mount, `--tmpfs /scratch`, lives in memory only. We wrote a file to one, restarted the container, and the folder was empty again. Use it for scratch files and secrets that must never reach a disk.

sections.h: How containers talk: the default bridge
sections.body:
Every container gets its own network namespace, so it has its own network card, IP address and `localhost`. Inside a container, `localhost` means that container itself, never your Mac and never another container. To reach a service on your Mac from a container, Docker Desktop offers the special name `host.docker.internal`.

Docker connects containers through a bridge, a virtual network switch inside the Linux VM. Any container you start without `--network` joins the default network, called `bridge`, and gets an address such as `172.17.0.5`.

The default bridge is old and limited:

- Containers can reach each other only by IP address. `ping b` from container `a` printed `ping: bad address 'b'`, while `ping 172.17.0.5` worked.
- Those addresses change when containers restart, so you cannot hard-code them.
- Every container started without `--network` lands on it, so unrelated apps can talk to each other.

For DNS, containers on the default bridge get a copy of the host's DNS settings. That lets them resolve names on the internet, but not each other. Docker's own docs say user-defined networks are better, and the next section shows why.

sections.h: User-defined networks: names that work
sections.body:
Create a network with `docker network create demo` and start containers with `--network demo`. Three things improve at once:

- Every container gets a DNS server at `127.0.0.11`, Docker's embedded DNS server. It answers with the current IP of any container on the same network, by name.
- Containers on different user-defined networks cannot reach each other, so each app gets its own private network.
- You can attach a running container to a network, or detach it, with `docker network connect` and `docker network disconnect`.

In the worked example, `wget http://web` from a container on `demo` returned the page, and `cat /etc/resolv.conf` showed `nameserver 127.0.0.11`. The same request from a container on the default bridge failed with `bad address 'web'`.

A container can sit on several networks, with one network card for each. That is how you build a proxy that talks to the outside on one network and to private services on another. The flag `--network-alias api` gives a container an extra DNS name on a network, which helps when one name should point at several containers.

Docker picks a private subnet for each network. Ours got `172.23.0.0/16`, while the default bridge used `172.17.0.0/16`. Both sit inside the private `172.16.0.0/12` range from Day 8, so they never clash with addresses on the internet.

Containers on the same network reach each other on any port. They need no `-p` at all, because `-p` is only for traffic from outside. Docker Compose creates one user-defined network per project, so everything in Day 15 gets name lookup for free.

sections.h: The host and none drivers, and publishing versus exposing
sections.body:
`bridge` is one of several network drivers. Two more matter on day one:

- `--network none` gives a container no network at all. `ip addr` inside showed only the loopback `lo`. Good for batch jobs that must not talk to anything.
- `--network host` skips the namespace and shares the host's network, so `-p` is ignored. On Docker Desktop it is off by default: you turn it on under Settings, Resources, Network, and you must be signed in.

Others, such as `overlay`, `macvlan` and `ipvlan`, connect containers across machines or straight onto a physical network. You will not need them for this course.

Publishing and exposing sound alike and do different things:

- `EXPOSE 80` in a Dockerfile is documentation. `docker image inspect nginx` lists `{"80/tcp":{}}`, and nothing listens on your Mac because of it.
- `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` publishes: it opens port 8080 on your Mac and forwards it. `docker port` then prints `80/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8080`.
- `-P` publishes every exposed port on a random free port of the host.

A common mistake is to publish ports just so two containers can talk. Put them on one user-defined network instead, and publish only what a person or another machine must reach.

lessons.analogy: Think of an office building. The default bridge is an open-plan floor with no phone directory. You can call a colleague only if you know their extension number, and the numbers change when people move desks. A user-defined network is a floor with a receptionist who knows everyone on that floor by name. Volumes are the storage room in the basement: people come and go, and the boxes stay. The picture fails at the building's edge, because a volume stays on the one Docker host where it was made and does not follow your container to another machine.

code.title: docker/network-demo.sh (in the lab repo)
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Day 14: containers find each other by name only on a user-defined network.
# Run it from anywhere: bash docker/network-demo.sh
# It removes everything it creates, even if a step fails.
set -euo pipefail

P=${PREFIX:-demo}   # name prefix, so the demo never clashes with your own containers
A="$P-a" B="$P-b" NET="$P-net"

cleanup() {
  docker rm -f "$A" "$B" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  docker network rm "$NET" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}
trap cleanup EXIT
cleanup

echo "1. Two containers on the default bridge network:"
docker run -d --name "$A" alpine:3.22 sleep 300 >/dev/null
docker run -d --name "$B" alpine:3.22 sleep 300 >/dev/null
if docker exec "$A" ping -c 1 -W 2 "$B" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "   $A reached $B by name"
else
  echo "   $A could not find $B by name"
fi

echo "2. Connect both to a user-defined network and try again:"
docker network create "$NET" >/dev/null
docker network connect "$NET" "$A"
docker network connect "$NET" "$B"
if docker exec "$A" ping -c 1 -W 2 "$B" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "   $A reached $B by name"
else
  echo "   $A could not find $B by name"
fi

echo "3. The DNS server $A asks now:"
docker exec "$A" grep nameserver /etc/resolv.conf | sed 's/^/   /'

code.title: docker/volume-backup.sh (in the lab repo)
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Day 14: back up a named volume to a .tgz file in this folder, or restore one.
#   bash docker/volume-backup.sh backup  <volume>
#   bash docker/volume-backup.sh restore <volume> <file.tgz>
# A short-lived alpine container mounts the volume and runs tar.
set -euo pipefail

action=${1:-}
volume=${2:-}

case "$action" in
  backup)
    # Stop here if the volume does not exist. Otherwise docker run would
    # quietly create a new, empty one and back that up.
    docker volume inspect "$volume" >/dev/null
    file="$volume-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).tgz"
    docker run --rm -v "$volume":/data:ro -v "$PWD":/backup alpine:3.22 \
      tar czf "/backup/$file" -C /data .
    echo "Saved $file"
    ;;
  restore)
    file=${3:?give the .tgz file to restore, from this folder}
    docker run --rm -v "$volume":/data -v "$PWD":/backup:ro alpine:3.22 \
      tar xzf "/backup/$file" -C /data
    echo "Restored $file into volume $volume"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "Usage: $0 backup <volume> | restore <volume> <file.tgz>" >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

interview.q: When would you use a volume, a bind mount or a tmpfs mount?
interview.a: I use a named volume for data the app owns, such as database files: Docker manages it and it outlives the container. I use a bind mount when I and the container both need the files, such as source code during development. I use tmpfs for scratch files or secrets that should never touch a disk. In production, bind mounts tie a container to one machine's folders, so they are rare there.

interview.q: Why should containers use a user-defined network instead of the default bridge?
interview.a: A user-defined network gives every container Docker's embedded DNS server, so containers find each other by name instead of by changing IP addresses. It also isolates the app, because containers on other networks cannot reach it. You can connect and disconnect running containers too. The default bridge has none of that, and every container started without --network shares it.

deeper.body:
In the hands-on task, the count survived the Redis swap because of how Redis saves its data. A rougher stop would have lost some of it.

Redis keeps its data in memory. It writes a snapshot file, `dump.rdb`, to `/data` from time to time, and again when it shuts down cleanly. To see the rules, set up the hands-on task again up to the step where you replace Redis, so Redis has had one clean stop. Run `docker exec redis redis-cli CONFIG GET save` and you get `3600 1 300 100 60 10000`. Read the numbers in pairs:

- after 3600 seconds, if at least 1 key changed
- after 300 seconds, if at least 100 keys changed
- after 60 seconds, if at least 10000 keys changed

In the task you used `docker stop`. That sends SIGTERM, Redis saves a final snapshot, and nothing is lost. Now try the rough way. Call the app a few more times, then run `docker rm -f redis`. The `-f` flag sends SIGKILL at once, so Redis has no chance to save. Start a fresh Redis on the same volume and call the app again. When we tried it, the count was 9 before the kill. The new Redis read the last snapshot, which said 5, so the four visits after that snapshot were lost.

That is the Day 6 lesson about signals, with real data at stake. In practice:

- Stop stateful containers with `docker stop` or `docker compose down`, both of which send SIGTERM first.
- For data you cannot lose, turn on Redis's append-only file with `--appendonly yes`, which logs every write.
- In production, consider a managed database service, where backups and failover are someone's full-time job.

The volume itself sits somewhere you might not expect. Run `docker volume inspect redis-data` (with Compose, the name is `hello-devops_redis-data`). It shows a mount point under `/var/lib/docker/volumes`. On a Mac, that path is inside Docker Desktop's Linux VM, so you will not find it in Finder. If you reset Docker Desktop to factory defaults, your volumes go with it.

sections.h: Compose describes the app you want
sections.body:
On Day 14 you wired up hello-devops and Redis by hand: a network, a volume and two long `docker run` commands, typed in the right order. That is imperative: you tell Docker each step. It works, and nobody wants to do it twice.

Docker Compose is declarative. You describe the finished app in one file, `compose.yaml`, and `docker compose up` works out the steps. Run it again and Compose changes only what differs from the file. Teammates get the same setup by cloning the repo.

The file format is the Compose Specification. Two version notes save confusion:

- The current tool is Compose v5. It works like Compose v2 and adds a Go library for other tools. The version number jumped to avoid confusion with the old file format versions.
- You will see `version: "3.8"` at the top of old files. Compose ignores that line, so leave it out.

Compose groups everything it creates into a project, named after the folder. In your `hello-devops` folder that gives a network called `hello-devops_default`, a volume called `hello-devops_redis-data` and containers called `hello-devops-web-1` and `hello-devops-redis-1`. The `-1` is a counter, because Compose can run several copies of one service.

sections.h: Reading the lab's compose.yaml
sections.body:
The lab's file, in the Files section, has two top-level keys. `services` holds one entry per container, and `volumes` declares the named volume. You do not declare a network: Compose creates one per project and puts every service on it, so service names work as DNS names, just like on Day 14.

Inside a service you will meet these keys:

- `build: .` builds the image from the Dockerfile in this folder. `image:` uses a ready-made image instead, such as `redis:8-alpine`.
- `ports:` publishes ports, written `"HOST:CONTAINER"` in quotes so YAML does not misread them.
- `environment:` sets env vars. `env_file:` reads them from a file instead.
- `volumes:` mounts named volumes or folders, as `redis-data:/data`.
- `depends_on:` controls start order, with an optional health condition.
- `healthcheck:` tells Docker how to test the container.
- `restart:` says what to do when the process stops.

Notice what the web service says: `REDIS_HOST: redis`. Redis has no `ports:` entry, because only web talks to it, over the project network. Only port 8000 is open to your Mac.

sections.h: Running is not ready: depends_on and healthchecks
sections.body:
`depends_on` makes Compose start Redis before web. In its short form, `depends_on: [redis]`, it only waits until the Redis container is running. A database can need several more seconds before it accepts connections, so running is not the same as ready.

A healthcheck closes that gap. It is a command Docker runs inside the container on a schedule, and exit code 0 means healthy (the exit codes from Day 6). The lab runs `redis-cli ping` every 5 seconds, with a 3-second timeout and 5 retries. The long form of `depends_on` then waits for it:

- `condition: service_healthy` waits until the healthcheck passes.
- `condition: service_completed_successfully` waits until a one-off job, such as a database migration, exits with 0.
- `condition: service_started` is the short form's behaviour.

In the worked example, `docker compose up -d` showed Redis as `Healthy` after 5.8 seconds and started web only then. `docker compose ps` shows `(health: starting)`, then `(healthy)`, or `(unhealthy)` if the check keeps failing.

This only covers startup. When Redis dies later, hello-devops answers `/readyz` with a 503, and `/` returns a 500 error until Redis is back. Your app must still cope when a dependency fails, and Kubernetes uses that readiness answer on Day 35.

sections.h: The everyday commands, and restart policies
sections.body:
These commands cover most days, run in the folder with `compose.yaml`:

- `docker compose up -d` creates and starts everything in the background; add `--build` to rebuild images first.
- `docker compose ps` shows each container, its health and its ports.
- `docker compose logs -f web` follows one service's output.
- `docker compose exec redis redis-cli GET visits` runs a command in a running service.
- `docker compose run --rm redis redis-cli -h redis ping` starts a new one-off container for a command, then removes it.
- `docker compose down` removes the containers and the network, and keeps named volumes.
- `docker compose down -v` also deletes the named volumes, and with them your data.
- `docker compose config` prints the final file after merging and filling in variables.

A restart policy says what Docker does when a container's process stops:

- `no`, the default: leave it stopped.
- `on-failure`: start it again only if it exited with a non-zero code.
- `always`: always start it again.
- `unless-stopped`: like always, except after you stopped it yourself.

The override file in this lesson sets `unless-stopped`. We shut Redis down from inside with `redis-cli shutdown`. Docker started it again within seconds, its restart count went to 1, and the visit count carried on.

sections.h: Variables: .env, environment and env_file
sections.body:
Compose can fill in placeholders in the file itself. Take `GREETING: "${GREETING:-Hello from Compose}"`. Compose looks for `GREETING` in your shell, then in a file named `.env` next to `compose.yaml`, and uses the default after `:-` if neither has it. We checked all three with `docker compose config | grep GREETING`:

1. With nothing set, it printed `GREETING: Hello from Compose`.
2. With `GREETING=Hi from .env` in `.env`, it printed `Hi from .env`.
3. With `GREETING='Hi from my shell'` before the command, the shell won.

Two files with similar names do different jobs, and this trips most people up:

- `.env` fills in `${...}` placeholders in the Compose file. Its values do not reach containers unless the file passes them on.
- `env_file: web.env` under a service sends every line of that file into the container as environment variables.

If `.env` ever holds secrets, keep it out of git; the lab's `.gitignore` already lists it. When something looks wrong, run `docker compose config` first. It shows the file exactly as Compose will use it.

sections.h: Override files and profiles
sections.body:
Compose reads `compose.yaml` and then, if it exists, `compose.override.yaml` from the same folder, and merges the two. That lets the base file stay simple and shared, while the override adds things only your laptop needs. The merge follows a few rules:

- A single value, such as `image` or `command`, is replaced by the override.
- Maps, such as `environment`, are merged key by key.
- Some lists, such as `ports`, are joined, so an override cannot remove a published port.
- Paths are relative to the first file, the base one.

`-f` picks files by hand. `docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d` uses only the base file, which is what CI should run. `-f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml` stacks another file on top.

A profile keeps a service switched off until you ask for it. The lab's override adds nginx in front of web, the reverse proxy you built on Day 9, with `profiles: ["proxy"]`. Plain `docker compose up -d` ignores it; `docker compose --profile proxy up -d` starts it too. Use profiles for extras such as a proxy, a database admin tool or a load generator.

One gotcha we hit while testing: plain `docker compose down` left the proxy running, and Compose reported that the network was still in use. Stop profiled services with the same `--profile` flag you started them with.

sections.h: Compose Watch for a fast inner loop
sections.body:
The inner loop is the cycle you repeat all day: edit, run, look. With plain Compose, every code change means `docker compose up -d --build`. Compose Watch shortens that. You list paths under `develop.watch` in the Compose file, run `docker compose watch`, and Compose reacts to every save:

- `sync` copies the changed files into the running container. Good for apps that reload code by themselves.
- `sync+restart` copies the files, then restarts the container. Good for gunicorn without reload.
- `rebuild` builds a new image and replaces the container. Use it for `requirements.txt`, because new packages need a new image.

The lab's override uses `sync+restart` for `app.py` and `rebuild` for `requirements.txt`. We changed the reply of `/healthz` while watch ran. It printed `Syncing service "web" after 1 changes were detected`, restarted web, and the next curl showed the new reply. The copied file arrived owned by the container's user, so it works with the non-root image from Day 16 too.

Why not a bind mount of the whole folder? It works, but on a Mac every file read crosses into the VM, and a bind mount also hides what the image had at that path. Watch copies only what changed and keeps the image's files. Keep bind mounts for files you want both sides to edit.

lessons.analogy: compose.yaml is like the stage plan a band sends to a venue. It lists each musician (service) and their instruments (images). It says who must be on stage and tuned before the show starts (depends_on with a health condition), and which microphones face the audience (ports). The crew reads the plan and sets the stage, and `down` clears it while the storage room (volumes) keeps its boxes. The picture fails on improvising: a stage crew adapts on the night, while Compose only does exactly what the file says, and only on one machine.

code.title: compose.yaml (the lab's file)
code.src:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      APP_VERSION: "1.0.0"
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  redis-data:

code.title: compose.override.yaml (lab: docker/compose.override.yaml; copy it next to compose.yaml)
code.src:
# Local development extras for compose.yaml (Day 15).
# Copy this file next to compose.yaml. Compose then merges it in by itself
# on every "docker compose" command. CI runs "docker compose -f compose.yaml"
# to leave it out.
services:
  web:
    environment:
      # From your shell or a .env file, with a default after ":-".
      GREETING: "${GREETING:-Hello from Compose}"
    # Start again if the process stops, unless you stopped it yourself.
    restart: unless-stopped
    develop:
      watch:
        # Copy app.py into the running container, then restart it.
        - action: sync+restart
          path: ./app.py
          target: /app/app.py
        # A new dependency needs a new image.
        - action: rebuild
          path: ./requirements.txt

  redis:
    restart: unless-stopped

  # nginx in front of web, like the reverse proxy from Day 9.
  # It only starts when you ask for it: docker compose --profile proxy up -d
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.31-alpine
    profiles: ["proxy"]
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./docker/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - web

task.title: Write the Compose files yourself and use them for development
steps: In your hello-devops repo, write `compose.yaml` from scratch: a `web` service built from your Dockerfile and a `redis` service from `redis:8-alpine` with a named volume at `/data`.
Publish port 8000 for web only, set `REDIS_HOST` and `APP_VERSION`, and give redis a healthcheck that web waits for.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences what `docker compose up -d` does for hello-devops, and why the visit count survives `docker compose down`. Mention the project network, depends_on and the volume.
explain_back.answer: Compose reads compose.yaml and the override, then creates a project network, a named volume and the containers. Because web depends on redis with condition service_healthy, it starts Redis first and waits until `redis-cli ping` passes. Docker's DNS on the project network turns the service name redis into the Redis container's IP, so `REDIS_HOST=redis` is enough. Redis keeps its data in the named volume, and `docker compose down` removes containers and the network but not named volumes, so the count is still there next time.

recap: compose.yaml describes the whole app; docker compose up makes reality match it.
Every project gets its own network, so service names work as hostnames.
depends_on waits for running; add a healthcheck and service_healthy to wait for ready.
`docker compose down` keeps named volumes; `down -v` deletes them.
.env fills placeholders in the file; env_file sends variables into the container.
Override files, profiles and watch keep the base file simple and the dev loop fast.

check.q: A compose.yaml uses `depends_on: [db]` in the short form, and db has no healthcheck. What does Compose wait for before starting the app?
options: The database to accept connections
The db container to be running, not ready
The db healthcheck to pass
Nothing; the start order is random
check.why: The short form only orders container starts; waiting for readiness needs a healthcheck and condition: service_healthy.

check.q: Your compose.yaml says `image: "shop:${TAG:-dev}"`. The `.env` file says `TAG=1.4`, and you run `TAG=1.5 docker compose up -d`. Which image runs?
options: shop:1.5
shop:1.4
shop:dev
Compose stops with an error about two values
check.why: A variable from your shell wins over the .env file, and the default after :- is used only when neither sets it.

check.q: A teammate adds an `adminer` database tool to compose.override.yaml with `profiles: ["tools"]`. In CI, the pipeline runs `docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d`. Does adminer start in CI?
options: Yes, because profiles start by default
Yes, because CI merges every Compose file
No, because CI never reads the override file
No, because Compose cannot run database tools
check.why: With -f compose.yaml the override file is not read at all, and a service in a profile only starts when that profile is asked for.

interview.q: Is Docker Compose suitable for production?
interview.a: For local development, demos and CI test setups, Compose works very well: one file, one command. It runs containers on a single host, so it cannot spread them over several machines or move them when a machine dies. Some small apps do run with Compose on one server, and Docker documents how to do that. Most teams use Kubernetes or a managed container service in production, and the images stay the same either way.

interview.q: How do you make one service wait until another is really ready in Compose?
interview.a: Plain `depends_on` only waits until the other container is running. I give the dependency a healthcheck, such as `pg_isready` for Postgres or `redis-cli ping` for Redis, and use `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`. For one-off jobs such as migrations, `service_completed_successfully` waits for a clean exit. The app should still retry and report itself unready, because dependencies can fail after startup too.

interview.q: How do you keep one Compose setup for both laptops and CI?
interview.a: I keep a lean, shared compose.yaml and put laptop-only settings, such as watch, debug tools and friendly defaults, in compose.override.yaml, which Compose merges automatically. CI runs `docker compose -f compose.yaml`, so it never sees the override, and can add its own file with a second `-f`. Optional extras go behind profiles. `docker compose config` shows the merged result whenever someone is unsure what will run.

deeper.body:
Compose Watch is easiest to understand by watching its output. With the lab's override in place, run `docker compose watch` in one terminal. It builds the image, starts the stack, then prints `Watch enabled` and waits. In a second terminal, change the reply of `/healthz` in app.py and save. These are the last lines watch printed in our test:

- `Container hello-devops-web-1 Started`
- `Watch enabled`
- `Syncing service "web" after 1 changes were detected`
- `Container hello-devops-web-1 Restarting`
- `Container hello-devops-web-1 Started`
- `service(s) ["web"] restarted`

Two details matter for real projects. First, list paths you never want copied under `ignore:` in each watch entry, such as test folders. Second, Docker's docs advise against syncing a dependency folder such as `node_modules`; let a `rebuild` rule install dependencies inside the image instead.

CI wants a different thing from Compose. It needs the stack started, and a fast failure if something is not healthy. The command `docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --wait` returns only when every service with a healthcheck is healthy, and fails if one becomes unhealthy. That makes it a good first step before integration tests.

You might try `docker compose up -d --scale web=3` to get three copies of web. With the lab's file it fails, because each copy would want host port 8000. The fix is to stop publishing web and let the nginx proxy be the only published service. Then nginx reaches the web copies by the name `web` over the project network. Kubernetes does this job properly on Day 33 with a Service.

Large setups split Compose files. `include:` pulls another Compose file into this one, and `extends:` reuses one service's settings in another. Docker's [guide to Compose in production](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/production/) explains how teams use an extra file for server settings when they do run Compose on a server.
