options: Nowhere, because ARG values vanish after the build
In `docker history`, next to the steps that used it
Only in the build log on the machine that built it
Only if a later ENV line copies it into the image

terms.plain: A Dockerfile with several FROM lines, where only the last stage becomes the image you ship.
A self-contained folder of Python packages (a venv) that a program can use on its own.
A normal user (not user ID 0) that the app runs as, so a break-in gets fewer rights.
A command Docker runs inside a container on a schedule; exit code 0 means the app works.
A public ID for one known security bug in a piece of software, such as CVE-2025-47273.
A tool that lists the packages in an image and reports which ones have known CVEs.

A password or token a build step needs, passed in a way that never stores it in the image.

sections.h: Two stages: build with tools, ship without them
sections.body:
The Day 13 image has one stage, so everything used to build the app ships with it. pip is there, and so is anything a compiler step would leave behind. None of it helps at run time. Each extra file is one more thing to patch, one more thing a scanner flags, and one more tool an attacker can use.

A multi-stage build fixes that. One Dockerfile holds several `FROM` lines, and each starts a new stage from a clean base. A later stage copies what it needs from an earlier one with `COPY --from=<stage>`. Only the last stage becomes the image. The others stay behind in the build cache.

The lab's final Dockerfile, in Files, has two stages:

1. `build` starts from `python:3.14-slim`, makes a virtual environment in `/venv`, installs the requirements into it, and removes pip from it.
2. The final stage starts from a fresh `python:3.14-slim`, removes the base image's own pip, and copies in `/venv` and `app.py`.

A virtual environment, or venv, is a folder that holds a set of Python packages. That makes it easy to move: one `COPY --from=build /venv /venv` brings every installed package across. `ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH"` makes the venv's `gunicorn` the one that runs.

For this small Python app the size barely moves: the content size went from 51.8 MB to 49.6 MB. The gain is in what is missing. For a Kotlin service the difference is large, because the build stage holds a JDK and Gradle and the final stage needs only a Java runtime and the jar. Day 24 builds exactly that.

sections.h: Choosing and pinning a base image
sections.body:
The base image decides most of what is in your image, and so most of what a scanner finds. For a Python app the usual choices are:

- `python:3.14`: full Debian with compilers and many tools. Big, and easy to debug.
- `python:3.14-slim`: Debian with only what Python needs. The lab uses this one.
- `python:3.14-alpine`: Alpine Linux, which uses a smaller C library called musl. Some packages with C code need extra work there.
- Distroless images: only the runtime, with no shell and no package manager.
- Docker Hardened Images (Day 12): distroless runtime images plus `-dev` variants with a shell for build stages.

Smaller bases mean fewer packages, faster pulls and shorter scan reports. The price is comfort. With no shell inside, `docker exec web sh` has nothing to run, so you need other ways to look inside.

Then pin what you chose. A tag moves when the publisher pushes an update, so `FROM python:3.14-slim` can mean different bytes next week. Add the digest to fix it: `FROM python:3.14-slim@sha256:cd89c30e...`, written with all 64 characters. The worked example shows how to find it. Every build then starts from exactly the same base. The catch is that security fixes stop arriving by themselves. Teams let a bot such as Dependabot or Renovate open a pull request when a new digest appears, and review it like any other change.

sections.h: Run as a normal user
sections.body:
A container runs as root, user ID 0, unless the image says otherwise. The Day 13 image did: `whoami` printed `root`. Namespaces fence the process in, but it is still root on a shared kernel. If an attacker breaks out through a bug in the kernel or in Docker, they arrive with root's rights.

Two lines in the final stage fix it:

- `RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home appuser` creates a normal user with no home folder.
- `USER 10001` makes every later step, and the running container, use that user.

Write the number in `USER`, not the name. Kubernetes can then check that an image runs as non-root without looking inside it. The files you copied in still belong to root, so the app can read its own code but cannot change it. That is what you want.

The missing home folder has one side effect. Gunicorn 26 tries to open a control socket, a special file that other programs can use to send it commands, in the user's home folder. Without the flag, our test container logged `Control server error: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/home/appuser'` at startup. The app still answered, but every start began with an error. The lab's `CMD` adds `--no-control-socket`, which turns that feature off.

sections.h: Tell Docker how to test the app
sections.body:
`docker ps` says `Up` as long as the main process lives. A process can be alive and still broken, for example stuck or failing every request. A `HEALTHCHECK` instruction tells Docker how to test the app from inside the container.

The lab's check runs a one-line Python command every 30 seconds that requests `/healthz`, with a 3-second timeout. It uses Python because the slim image has no curl. Exit code 0 counts as a pass, and anything else as a failure. The status moves through three states:

1. `starting`, until the first check has run.
2. `healthy`, once a check passes.
3. `unhealthy`, after 3 failures in a row, the default.

`docker inspect -f '{{json .State.Health}}' web` shows the latest results with their exit codes and output.

Who acts on the status matters:

- Plain Docker only reports it. It does not restart an unhealthy container.
- Compose uses it for `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` (Day 15).
- Kubernetes ignores `HEALTHCHECK`. It has its own probes, which Day 35 points at the same `/healthz` and `/readyz` endpoints.

Keep the check cheap and local. It should test that this process can answer, not that every database behind it is up.

sections.h: Scanning: less inside means less to patch
sections.body:
A CVE is a public ID for one known security bug, such as `CVE-2025-47273`. A vulnerability scanner lists every package in an image and checks each one against databases of CVEs. Two scanners are worth knowing:

- Trivy, an open source scanner. Install it with `brew install trivy`.
- Docker Scout, which comes with Docker Desktop: `docker scout quickview` gives a summary, and `docker scout cves` the full list.

Read the results with care. Each finding has a severity from LOW to CRITICAL, and a status:

- `fixed` means a newer version of the package fixes the bug. You can act on it.
- `affected` means no fix exists yet. You can only wait and rebuild.

On the day we scanned, all 44 HIGH findings in the Debian base were unfixed, and `--ignore-unfixed` dropped them to zero. Those come from the base image, so the fix is to rebuild once Debian ships patched packages. A smaller base would have fewer of them to begin with.

Removing pip took away 5 more HIGH findings. They sat in libraries that pip carries inside itself, such as urllib3 and msgpack. The app never runs pip, so the lab uninstalls it in both stages.

New CVEs are published every day, so your numbers will differ from ours. That is why CI scans on every build, which Day 52 sets up.

sections.h: Two CPU types, and a push to GHCR
sections.body:
Your Mac builds arm64 images, and most servers run amd64. The command `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` builds both and pushes one index with a manifest for each, as on Day 12. The `RUN` steps for the other CPU type run through emulation, so the amd64 half of the build is slower on your Mac.

GitHub Container Registry, `ghcr.io`, keeps images next to your code. Pushing there takes three things:

1. A personal access token (classic) with the `write:packages` scope. GitHub Packages accepts only classic tokens.
2. `docker login ghcr.io -u <your-github-user> --password-stdin`, with the token piped in so it never appears in your shell history.
3. An image name of the form `ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/hello-devops:1.0.0`.

Two details save you a search later:

- A new package on GHCR is private at first. You can change its visibility in the package settings.
- The label `org.opencontainers.image.source`, set to your repo's URL, links the package to the repo.

A token on your laptop is fine for one manual push. Day 21 moves this push into GitHub Actions, which uses a short-lived token instead.

sections.h: Secrets at build time
sections.body:
Sometimes a build step needs a secret, such as a token to download a private package. The obvious ways all leak:

- `ARG` with `--build-arg`: `docker history` shows the value.
- `ENV`: the value is stored in the image config, so anyone who pulls the image can read it.
- `COPY` a token file and `RUN rm` it later: the file stays in its layer, as Day 12 showed.

In the worked example, `docker history` printed our fake token twice for the `ARG` version.

BuildKit has a safe way. `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=api_token,env=API_TOKEN` hands the secret to that one `RUN` step, as an environment variable. Leave out `env=` and it appears as a file under `/run/secrets/` instead. You pass the secret to the build in one of two ways:

- `--secret id=api_token,env=API_TOKEN` reads it from your shell's environment.
- `--secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc` reads it from a file.

The value never lands in a layer, the cache or the history. Run-time secrets, such as a database password, are a separate problem. They come from the environment when the container starts, never from the image. Day 34 shows how Kubernetes handles them.

code.title: Dockerfile (the lab's final version)
code.src:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- build stage: install dependencies into a virtual environment ----
FROM python:3.14-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
RUN python -m venv /venv
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH"
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
# pip is only needed to install packages. Remove it from the venv we ship.
RUN pip uninstall -y pip

# ---- run stage: only what the app needs at run time ----
FROM python:3.14-slim
# The base image has its own pip. The app does not need it, so remove it too.
RUN pip uninstall -y pip
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /venv /venv
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH" PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
COPY app.py .
# The version is baked in at build time: docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.2.0 .
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION
# Run as a normal user, not root.
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home appuser
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz')"
# --no-control-socket: Gunicorn 26 would otherwise try to open a socket in a home folder this user does not have.
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "2", "--no-control-socket", "app:app"]

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate in 3 to 4 sentences what makes the lab's final image safer than the Day 13 image. Mention the stages, the user, pip and the health check.
explain_back.answer: The final Dockerfile installs packages into a venv in a build stage and copies only that venv and app.py into a fresh final stage, so build leftovers never ship. It removes pip from both the venv and the base, which took away five known CVEs that pip carried with it. The app runs as user 10001 instead of root, so a break-in gets far fewer rights. A HEALTHCHECK lets Docker and Compose see whether the app actually answers, not only whether its process is alive.

check.q: A Go team's single-stage image is 900 MB because it contains the Go compiler and module cache. Which change shrinks it the most?
options: Add the module cache folder to .dockerignore
Delete the compiler in a later RUN step
Build the binary in one stage, copy it into a small one
Build with --no-cache so old layers are not reused
check.why: Only the last stage ships, so the compiler and cache stay in the build stage; deleting them later only hides them in an earlier layer.

check.q: A build must read `~/.npmrc`, which holds a token, to install private packages. Which approach keeps the token out of the image?
options: COPY .npmrc, install, then RUN rm .npmrc
Pass it with --secret and a RUN --mount=type=secret step
Set ENV NPM_TOKEN in the build stage only
Read it in an ARG and unset it after the install
check.why: A secret mount exists only during that RUN step and is never written to a layer, the cache or the history.

check.q: A scan reports 30 HIGH CVEs, all with status `affected` and no fixed version, in your Debian base image. What is the sensible next step?
options: Add an apt-get upgrade step and ship today
Stop scanning, because the results cannot be fixed
Rewrite the app in another language
Track them, rebuild when fixes ship, and consider a smaller base
check.why: No patched package exists yet, so an upgrade changes nothing; you rebuild when one ships, and a smaller base has fewer such packages at all.

interview.q: What makes a container image production-ready?
interview.a: I build it in stages, so only the runtime and the app ship, from a small base pinned by digest. It runs as a numeric non-root user, has a health check, and holds no secrets: build secrets go through secret mounts and run-time secrets come from the environment. CI scans every build and fails on serious findings that have a fix. Finally it is tagged with a real version, pushed for every CPU type we run, and deployed by digest.

interview.q: Why should a container not run as root?
interview.a: Containers share the host's kernel, so root in a container is still root to that kernel, only fenced in by namespaces. If an attacker gets code running in the app and then finds a kernel or runtime bug, root makes the escape much worse. Running as a normal user also stops the app from changing its own code or installing tools. Writing the user as a number lets Kubernetes enforce non-root without inspecting the image.

interview.q: How do you give a Docker build a secret, such as a token for a private package registry?
interview.a: I use BuildKit secret mounts: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token,env=TOKEN` in the Dockerfile and `docker build --secret id=token,env=TOKEN` on the command line. The secret exists only while that one RUN step runs and never lands in a layer or the history. ARG, ENV and copying a file then deleting it all leave the value in the image. In CI the secret comes from the CI system's secret store, passed the same way.

deeper.body:
Three experiments take the lab's Dockerfile further.

First, the control socket. Run the final image with gunicorn started by hand and no `--no-control-socket` flag: `docker run -d --name nosock hello-devops:1.0.0 gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 app:app`. Then read `docker logs nosock`. Ours ended with `[ERROR] Control server error: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/home/appuser'`, while the container stayed up. That is the cost of a user with no home folder, and why the flag is in the lab's `CMD`. Remove it with `docker rm -f nosock`.

Second, a small waste we found in the final stage. In `docker history hello-devops:1.0.0`, the final stage's `RUN pip uninstall -y pip` layer is 4.85 MB. That is odd for a step that deletes things. Running pip makes Python save compiled `.pyc` files for every module it loads. The command `find /usr/local/lib/python3.14 -name '*.pyc' | wc -l` counted 0 in the base image and 150 in ours. Writing the line as `RUN PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 pip uninstall -y pip` stops that, and the same layer measured 28.7 kB. Try it and compare the two histories.

Third, a hardened base. Docker's migration guide for Python uses `dhi.io/python:3.13-alpine3.23-dev` for the build stage and `dhi.io/python:3.13-alpine3.23` for the final one. You need `docker login dhi.io` with a free Docker account first. Moving the lab to such a base changes four things:

- The final stage has no shell, so shell-form `RUN` lines there fail. Drop the `pip uninstall` and `useradd` lines.
- The runtime image already runs as a non-root user and, by Docker's docs, has no package manager.
- The lab's `HEALTHCHECK` is in shell form, which `docker history` shows as `CMD-SHELL`. It needs `/bin/sh`, so rewrite it in exec form as a JSON list.
- Debugging changes too: `docker exec web sh` has no shell to start.

We did not build this version here, because pulling from dhi.io needs a login. Read [Use a Docker Hardened Image](https://docs.docker.com/dhi/how-to/use/) before you try, and compare the scan results with your slim image.

recap: A container is a Linux process fenced in by namespaces and limited by cgroups; on a Mac it runs in a small Linux VM.
An image is read-only layers plus a config, named by digests; a container adds one writable layer.
Tags move and digests do not; one name can hold a variant for each CPU type.
A Dockerfile builds an image step by step; order the steps so the cache saves the slow ones.
Use exec form for CMD so the app is PID 1 and stops cleanly on SIGTERM.
Keep data in volumes, and connect containers on a user-defined network where names work.
compose.yaml describes the whole app; up, down, logs and config cover most days.
Production images are multi-stage, non-root, health-checked, scanned and free of secrets.

flashcards.front: What two Linux kernel features make a process a container?
flashcards.back: Namespaces (what it can see) and cgroups (how much CPU and memory it can use).

flashcards.front: Why does Docker Desktop on a Mac run a Linux VM?
flashcards.back: Containers need a Linux kernel, and macOS does not have one.

flashcards.front: In `-p 8080:80`, which number is on your Mac?

flashcards.back: The process was killed with SIGKILL (128 + 9), often after ignoring SIGTERM.

flashcards.front: What is an image made of?
flashcards.back: Read-only layers, a config and a manifest that lists them by digest.

flashcards.front: Why does deleting a file in a later Dockerfile step not shrink the image?
flashcards.back: The file stays in the earlier layer; the later layer only hides it.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a tag and a digest?
flashcards.back: A tag is a movable name; a digest is the hash of the content and never changes.

flashcards.front: What does `docker buildx imagetools inspect` show without pulling?
flashcards.back: An image's digest and the platforms in its index.

flashcards.front: When does Docker rebuild a cached Dockerfile step?
flashcards.back: When that step or anything before it changed; then every later step rebuilds too.

flashcards.front: CMD or ENTRYPOINT: which one do docker run arguments replace?
flashcards.back: CMD. Arguments are added after ENTRYPOINT.

flashcards.front: Which one reaches the running container: ARG or ENV?
flashcards.back: ENV. ARG exists only during the build.

flashcards.front: Inside a container, what does localhost mean?
flashcards.back: The container itself, never your Mac or another container.

flashcards.front: What do user-defined networks have that the default bridge lacks?
flashcards.back: Docker's DNS server at 127.0.0.11, so containers find each other by name.

flashcards.front: What does `docker compose down -v` delete that `down` keeps?
flashcards.back: The named volumes, and the data in them.

flashcards.front: How do you make a Compose service wait until Redis is ready?
flashcards.back: Give Redis a healthcheck and use depends_on with condition: service_healthy.

flashcards.front: How do you pass a token to a build without storing it?
flashcards.back: RUN --mount=type=secret in the Dockerfile and docker build --secret.

quiz.q: Two containers from the same image both write to /tmp/cache.txt. What does each container see?
options: The last write from either container
Only its own file, in its own writable layer
An error, because image files are read-only
A shared file that both can append to
quiz.why: Each container gets its own writable layer on top of the shared image layers, so their changes never meet.

quiz.q: A Dockerfile copies the whole project with `COPY . .` before installing dependencies. A teammate fixes a typo in README.md. What happens on the next build?
options: Nothing rebuilds, because README.md is not code
Only the COPY step reruns; the install stays cached
Docker reruns the COPY, the install and every later step
Docker re-downloads the base image
quiz.why: The copied files changed, so that layer and every layer after it rebuild, unless .dockerignore leaves README.md out.

quiz.q: On an amd64 server, a container fails at once with `exec format error`. The image was built on a MacBook. What is the likely cause?
options: The image holds only arm64 code
The server is out of disk space
The image has no CMD instruction
The tag latest was not pushed
quiz.why: A Mac builds arm64 code by default; without an amd64 variant in the index, the server cannot run it.

quiz.q: A web container and a Postgres container run on a user-defined network. Which `-p` options do they need for the web app to reach the database?
options: -p 5432:5432 on the database
-p on both containers
-p 5432:5432 on the web container
None; -p is only for traffic from outside
quiz.why: Containers on one network reach each other on any port by name; publishing only matters for your Mac or other machines.

quiz.q: You run `docker compose down` and then `docker compose up -d`. Redis keeps its data in a named volume. What happens to the stored data?
options: It is gone, because down removes everything
It is still there, because named volumes survive down
It is restored from the image's VOLUME line
It survives only if you add --build
quiz.why: down removes containers and networks; named volumes stay until you add -v or remove them yourself.

quiz.q: A container's STATUS says `Up 5 minutes (unhealthy)`. What does plain Docker do about it?
options: It restarts the container at once
It removes the container and starts a new one
It stops sending traffic to the container
Nothing; it only reports the status
quiz.why: Standalone Docker records the health status but takes no action; Compose and other tools decide what to do with it.

quiz.q: Which Dockerfile line keeps a deploy repeatable even if someone pushes a new base image with the same tag?
options: FROM python:3.14-slim@sha256:<digest>
FROM python:latest
FROM python:3.14-slim AS base
FROM docker.io/library/python:3.14-slim
quiz.why: A digest names one exact image, while any tag can be moved to different content.

quiz.q: After a scan, 5 HIGH findings sit in libraries inside pip, and the app never uses pip at run time. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Mark them as accepted in the scanner
Upgrade pip in the final stage
Remove pip from the image you ship
Switch the scanner to a different tool
quiz.why: A package that is not in the image cannot be attacked or flagged, and the app does not need it.

quiz.q: A container runs as user 10001 and tries to write to a file owned by root with permissions rw-r--r-- (644). What happens?
options: The write works, because containers ignore permissions
The write fails with Permission denied
The write works only in the image layer
Docker changes the owner to 10001 first
quiz.why: Only the owner, root, has write permission; everyone else, including uid 10001, can only read.

quiz.q: An app inside a container listens on 127.0.0.1:8000, and you started it with `-p 8000:8000`. Why does curl from your Mac get no answer?
options: Port 8000 is reserved on macOS
The container needs EXPOSE 8000 as well
Docker blocks HTTP traffic by default
The app only accepts connections from inside the container
quiz.why: 127.0.0.1 is the container's own loopback; the app must bind 0.0.0.0 to accept traffic forwarded from outside.
